units.t: Anchoring: The First Number Wins.
Part one. The rigged wheel.
Let's start with a quick question.
Did Mahatma Gandhi die before or after the age of one hundred and forty?
Obviously before.
Now, roughly how old do you think he was when he died?
Hold your guess in your head for a moment.
In 1997, the German psychologists Fritz Strack and Thomas Mussweiler asked people almost exactly that.
One group was asked whether Gandhi died before or after the age of one hundred and forty.
Another group was asked whether he died before or after the age of nine.
Both questions are silly.
Nobody learns anything from them.
Yet when both groups were then asked for their best guess, the answers split apart.
The group that heard nine guessed, on average, about fifty.
The group that heard one hundred and forty guessed, on average, about sixty-seven.
Gandhi was actually seventy-eight.
That's anchoring.
When we have to estimate a number, the first number we come across tends to pull our estimate towards it, even when we know that number is meaningless.
The classic demonstration came from Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, in a famous paper published in 1974.
They showed people a wheel of fortune, marked from nought to one hundred.
What the participants didn't know was that the wheel was rigged to stop at either ten or sixty-five.
After the spin, people were asked what percentage of the countries in the United Nations were African.
Those who saw the wheel land on ten gave a typical answer of about twenty-five per cent.
Those who saw it land on sixty-five gave a typical answer of about forty-five per cent.
A random spin of a wheel shifted their answers by twenty points.
Later researchers pushed the idea even further.

In a study published in 2003, Dan Ariely, George Loewenstein and Drazen Prelec asked students at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to write down the last two digits of their American social security number.
Then the students bid on everyday items, such as a cordless keyboard, some chocolates and bottles of wine.
Students whose numbers happened to be high bid far more than students whose numbers were low.
For some items, the top group bid around three times as much as the bottom group.
An arbitrary number had set the price in their heads.
So anchors don't have to be relevant, and they don't have to be believable.
In the next part, we'll look at where anchors show up in everyday life, and why even experts fall for them.
Part two. Anchors all around you.
Once you know about anchoring, you start noticing anchors everywhere.
Take shopping.
A jacket marked was $300, now $149, feels like a bargain.
But the $300 is doing most of the work.
It sets the reference point, and $149 looks small next to it.
The same jacket simply priced at $149 would feel much more ordinary.
Menus do it too.
A very expensive dish near the top can make the other mains look reasonable by comparison, even if you'd never order it.
Some wine lists work the same way, with one eye-watering bottle that quietly makes the second cheapest look sensible.
Anchors are powerful in negotiations.
When you're buying a used car or selling a couch online, the first number put on the table tends to shape where the deal ends up.
Research by Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler found that whoever makes the first offer often gets a better result, because that offer becomes the anchor for everything that follows.
Sometimes the anchor is a number from your own past.
If you bought a house or a share at a certain price, that figure can stay lodged in your head for years.
Every later offer gets judged against it, even though the market has no idea what you paid.
The same thing happens with the price you remember paying for a coffee or a tank of petrol a few years ago.
An old number can make a fair price today feel like a rip-off, or a poor deal feel like a steal.
Surely experts are immune?
Not really.
In a study from 1987, Gregory Northcraft and Margaret Neale took real estate agents in Arizona through a house for sale and gave them a pack of information about it.
The only thing that changed between groups was the listing price in the pack.
The agents' own valuations moved up and down with that listing price.
And when asked, most of the agents said the listing price hadn't influenced them.
Perhaps the most unsettling study involved judges and prosecutors in Germany.
Birte Englich, Thomas Mussweiler and Fritz Strack gave experienced legal professionals a realistic shoplifting case.
Before deciding a sentence, each one rolled a pair of dice to get the prosecutor's demand.
The dice were loaded to land on either three or nine.
Those who rolled nine gave sentences of about eight months, on average.
Those who rolled three gave sentences of about five months.
These were trained professionals, and they knew the number came from dice.
Why is anchoring so hard to shake?
Researchers think two things are going on.
The first is that we start from the anchor and adjust away from it, but we stop too soon.
Once an answer feels plausible, we settle, and that's usually still on the anchor's side.
The second is that an anchor quietly primes the evidence we think about.
If someone asks whether a house is worth more than a million dollars, your mind starts looking for reasons it could be.
Those reasons then feel convincing when you make your own estimate.
So what can you do about something that works even on judges?
That's where we're going next.
Part three. Pulling up the anchor.
The honest news first.
Anchoring is one of the most stubborn biases in psychology.
Simply being warned about it doesn't make it go away.
But there are habits that weaken its grip.
The first habit is to set your own anchor before anyone else does.
Before you look at a price tag, a quote or an asking price, decide roughly what you think it's worth.
Before you walk into a car yard, check what similar cars have sold for.
Before you ask a tradie for a quote, have a rough idea of what the job usually costs.
If you arrive with your own number, the other person's number has less room to take over.
The second habit might sound familiar from the first episode of this series.
Consider the opposite.
In a study published in 2000, Thomas Mussweiler, Fritz Strack and Tim Pfeiffer asked car experts to value a used car after hearing a seller's price.
When the experts were first asked to list reasons why that price might be wrong, the anchor's pull shrank noticeably.
So when you hear a number, ask yourself, what are the reasons this might be too high, or too low?
That simple question makes you gather the evidence the anchor was steering you away from.
The third habit is to compare like with like.
In Australian supermarkets, the larger stores have to show a unit price on the shelf label, such as the price per hundred grams or per litre.
That little number is your friend.
It ignores the was price and the special sticker and tells you what you're actually paying.
The same idea works for bigger purchases.
Compare the actual cost with other options, not with the number the seller first showed you.
The fourth habit is to use anchors on purpose.
If you're selling something, it often pays to name a sensible but ambitious first number, rather than waiting to hear theirs.
And if someone throws out an outrageous anchor at you, don't just argue around it.
Name it, set it aside, and put your own number on the table.
Let's recap.
The first number we hear tends to drag our estimates towards it, even when it came from a wheel of fortune or a roll of the dice.
It works on shoppers, estate agents and judges, and being warned isn't enough to stop it.
Your best defences are to set your own number first, consider why the anchor might be wrong, and compare real costs rather than starting prices.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In the Gandhi study, what happened to people who first heard the number one hundred and forty?
Answer. They guessed he died older, at about sixty-seven, compared with about fifty for the group who heard nine.
Question two. In the German sentencing study, how was the prosecutor's demand decided?
Answer. By rolling loaded dice.
Question three. What's one good habit for resisting an anchor?
Answer. Set your own number first, or ask why the anchor might be wrong.
That's the end of Anchoring: The First Number Wins. Well done.
